meaning: “It's not as if ...”. Points out a premise that is clearly not true, then uses it to criticize, advise, or make a judgment.
connection: Noun + ではあるまいし／じゃあるまいし; Verb plain form + わけではあるまいし

senses.label: It's not as if you're ...
senses.meaning: First names an identity or situation that obviously doesn't apply. The speaker then follows with criticism, advice, or an opinion. The tone is irritated or reproachful, and it is mostly spoken.
senses.connection: Noun + ではあるまいし／じゃあるまいし (common: 「子供じゃあるまいし」, 「神様ではあるまいし」)
examples: You're not a child. Take care of your own things.
I'm not God. There's no way I could know the future.
You're not a student anymore. That kind of excuse won't fly.

senses.label: It's not as if ... is going to happen
senses.meaning: Follows 「わけ」 or 「の」 and rejects an exaggerated outcome: “it's not like ..., so there's no need to act like that”. Often used to comfort someone or tell them not to take it so hard.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + わけではあるまいし／わけじゃあるまいし
examples: It's not like you'll never see each other again. You don't have to cry so much.
It's not like you're going to die. Don't get down over one failure.

notes: The second half is usually a command, advice, criticism, or a judgment like 「〜はずがない」 or 「〜ことはない」. It can't be followed by a neutral, objective statement.
「〜ではあるまいし」 is stronger than 「〜ではないのだから」 and clearly carries irritation or sarcasm.
In speech, 「〜じゃあるまいし」 is common. 「〜でもあるまいし」 is also used.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ではあるまいか」 (“isn't it perhaps ...?”), which is a guess.

daily.title: A parent scolds a child
daily.description: A parent is annoyed with a child who is already grown up.
daily.example: You're in high school now, right? You're not a little kid. At least get yourself up in the morning.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Seeing off a friend who is going abroad to study.
daily.example: It's not like this is goodbye forever. We'll see each other again in the summer break.

daily.title: Pushing back on high expectations
daily.description: Someone expects you to predict the outcome.
daily.example: I'm not a fortune-teller. How would I know tomorrow's weather?

work.title: A senior warns a junior
work.description: A senior is annoyed with a coworker who has been there for a few years.
work.example: You're not a new hire anymore. A mistake like this is a problem.

work.title: Calming people down in a meeting
work.description: A coworker is overly worried about a small problem, and the manager tells them to stay calm.
work.example: It's not like the company is going under. Let's deal with this calmly.

etymology: From 「ではあるまい」 (“probably isn't”), the negative conjecture of 「である」, plus 「し」, which gives a reason. Literally “it probably isn't ..., so ...”, which became the set phrase “it's not as if ...”.

similar.title: 〜ではあるまいか
similar.explanation: 「〜ではあるまいか」 is a soft guess: “isn't it perhaps ...?”. 「〜ではあるまいし」 first denies a premise, then criticizes or advises.

similar.title: 〜からといって
similar.explanation: 「〜からといって」 means “just because ... doesn't mean ...”, and its first part is a fact. The first part of 「〜ではあるまいし」 is something clearly untrue.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「〜わけではない」 is a partial, objective denial. 「〜わけではあるまいし」 uses a denial to lead into advice and is emotional.

meaning: “I can't stand ...”. Says that a situation is unbearable and really bothering you.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective 〜くて + はかなわない; Noun + ではかなわない

senses.label: I can't stand ...
senses.meaning: Says that if a situation keeps up, you won't be able to take it. It has a complaining, dissatisfied tone. Often used with 「こう」, 「こんなに」, or 「毎日」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective 〜くて + はかなわない; Noun + ではかなわない (common: 「暑くてはかなわない」, 「〜されてはかなわない」)
examples: I can't stand it being this hot every day.
I can't take the people next door making noise until midnight.
Working overtime like this every single day is too much.

senses.label: Casual contractions
senses.meaning: In speech, 「ては」 often becomes 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 becomes 「じゃ」. 「ない」 can also become 「ん」, as in Kansai speech. The tone is more casual and the complaint more direct.
senses.connection: Verb te-form → 〜ちゃかなわない／〜じゃかなわない; 〜てはかなわん
examples: I can't stand getting called in every time I have a day off.
I can't live on a salary this low.
Having to give the same explanation every time is too much.

notes: 「かなわない」 originally means “can't beat” or “no match for”. Here it has shifted to “can't bear it”. It is usually written in kana.
It often goes with the passive (「〜されてはかなわない」) to say you are being bothered by what someone else does.
Different from 「〜てたまらない」: 「〜てたまらない」 is about your own strong feelings or sensations, while 「〜てはかなわない」 complains about an outside situation.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Complaining to family about the midsummer heat.
daily.example: Over 35 degrees day after day? I can't stand this heat.

daily.title: Noisy neighbors
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about noise from upstairs.
daily.example: The footsteps are loud until late every night. I can't take it.

daily.title: Grumbling at family
daily.description: A mother grumbles because her kids always leave things lying around.
daily.example: I can't stand you messing up the room every day.

work.title: Complaining among coworkers
work.description: Developers are fed up with constant spec changes.
work.example: I can't take them changing the specs over and over like this.

work.title: Sighing over a client's demands
work.description: Complaining privately about unreasonable demands.
work.example: I can't stand them calling late at night every day.

etymology: 「かなう（敵う・叶う）」 means “to match” or “to be equal to”. Its negative 「かなわない」 originally meant “can't beat”. Attached to the conditional 「〜ては」, it means “if this goes on, I can't bear it”, and so “I can't stand it”.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「〜てたまらない」 means your own feelings or sensations are too strong to hold back (「うれしくてたまらない」). 「〜てはかなわない」 is only for troublesome outside situations and carries a complaint.

similar.title: 〜ては (negative result)
similar.explanation: 「〜ては」 is a hypothetical condition that can lead to all kinds of negative results. 「〜てはかなわない」 is a set phrase that directly says “I can't stand it”.

similar.title: 〜てはいられない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはいられない」 means “I can't keep doing ...” and shows that you will stop doing something. 「〜てはかなわない」 is a complaint about a situation.

meaning: “Without hesitation; openly”. Says that someone openly says or does something eye-catching without any reserve.
connection: Verb te-form + はばからない

senses.label: Openly, without reserve
senses.meaning: Shows that someone speaks or acts openly without caring what others think. It is often used for bold, confident, or even off-putting words and actions. It carries the speaker's surprise or criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はばからない／はばからず (common: 「公言して」, 「断言して」, 「豪語して」, 「言って」)
examples: He openly declares that he is a genius.
That politician doesn't hesitate to say that a tax increase is unavoidable.
She boasted without reserve that she would definitely become company president one day.

notes: It is mostly used about a third person's words or actions and includes the speaker's evaluation. It is almost never used about yourself.
It most often goes with verbs of speaking like 「言う」, 「公言する」, 「断言する」, and 「豪語する」.
It is quite literary and common in news and opinion pieces. It can be written in kanji as 「憚らない」.
「人目をはばからず」 (“without caring who is watching”) is related, but it takes noun + を, so it is not this pattern.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: Talking about a very self-confident friend.
daily.example: That guy goes around saying he's the best chef in the world.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: A report on something a celebrity said.
daily.example: That actor openly says he has no interest in marriage.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a company leader's bold statement.
work.example: The company's chairman boasts without reserve that it will take the top spot in the industry.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A critic criticizes an official's attitude.
work.example: The minister flatly declared, without hesitation, that he was not responsible.

etymology: 「はばかる（憚る）」 means “to hold back out of respect or fear”. Its negative 「はばからない」 means “without any reserve”. After a verb te-form, it means doing something with no hesitation at all.

similar.title: 〜をものともせず
similar.explanation: 「〜をものともせず」 means not letting difficulty or danger stop you, and it is positive. 「〜てはばからない」 means not caring what others think and is usually critical.

similar.title: 〜を顧みず
similar.explanation: 「〜を顧みず」 means disregarding danger, family, and so on, and it follows a noun. 「〜てはばからない」 follows a verb te-form and focuses on open statements.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: 「〜もかまわず」 means not minding a situation (「人目もかまわず」). 「〜てはばからない」 stresses openly stating something.

meaning: “Sincerely; never stop ...”. Shows that a strong feeling continues and never stops.
connection: Verb te-form + やまない (with verbs of feeling)

senses.label: Sincerely wish
senses.meaning: Follows verbs like 「願う」, 「祈る」, 「期待する」, and 「望む」 to express a heartfelt wish. Used mostly in formal settings such as speeches and letters. The polite form is 「〜てやみません」.
senses.connection: 願って／祈って／期待して／望んで + やまない（やみません）
examples: I sincerely wish you all good health and happiness.
I pray with all my heart for peace to come to the world.
I have high hopes for all of you young people and your future success.

senses.label: Always; never stop ...
senses.meaning: Follows verbs like 「愛する」, 「尊敬する」, and 「魅了する」 to show that a feeling has lasted a long time and never changed. Often used to modify a noun.
senses.connection: 愛して／尊敬して／魅了して + やまない (+ Noun)
examples: He loved his hometown deeply all his life.
This painting still captivates many people today.
My teacher, whom I have always deeply respected, has passed away.

notes: It only follows verbs of feeling or wishing. It can't be used for ordinary actions (✕「雨が降ってやまない」).
The subject is usually the speaker. With a third person, it is often a “makes people ...” expression (「人々を魅了してやまない」).
It is written language, common in speeches, letters of congratulation, and the ends of essays. It can be written in kanji as 「止まない」 or 「已まない」.

daily.title: Wedding speech
daily.description: A friend gives a speech at a wedding to bless the couple.
daily.example: I sincerely wish you both lasting happiness.

daily.title: Reading a magazine
daily.description: Reading a profile in a magazine.
daily.example: She has loved music deeply ever since she was little.

work.title: Closing a congratulatory letter
work.description: A company sends a letter of congratulations to a business partner.
work.example: We sincerely wish your company continued prosperity.

work.title: Graduation speech
work.description: The principal shares hopes for the graduates.
work.example: I sincerely wish every one of our graduates a future full of happiness.

etymology: 「やむ（止む）」 means “to stop”. 「〜てやまない」 literally means “... and does not stop”, so it shows a feeling that keeps going. It is a set expression of written Japanese.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: 「〜てならない」 means a feeling wells up naturally and can't be held back (often negative), and is also used in speech. 「〜てやまない」 is mostly for positive wishes or admiration and is written style.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「〜てたまらない」 stresses that a feeling or sensation is intense right now, and can be used for physical sensations. 「〜てやまない」 stresses that a feeling lasts a long time and is for formal settings.

meaning: “Combined with ...”. Shows that two factors work together to produce a stronger effect.
connection: Noun + と相まって／も相まって; AとBが相まって

senses.label: Combining with each other
senses.meaning: Shows that A and B work together to bring about a result. The result can be good or bad. Written style.
senses.connection: AとBが相まって／AがBと相まって (common: 「〜と相まって、〜効果を生む」)
examples: The beautiful scenery combined with the delicious food made it an unforgettable trip.
His talent, combined with hard work, came into full bloom.

senses.label: With the added factor of ...
senses.meaning: 「〜も相まって」 means “with ... added on top”, which makes an existing situation even more noticeable. Often used to explain a cause.
senses.connection: Noun + も相まって (common: 「好天も相まって」, 「円安も相まって」)
examples: Helped by the good weather, the venue was packed with people.
With the weak yen adding to it, the number of foreign tourists is rising sharply.

notes: 「相まって」 is also written 「あいまって」. Don't confuse it with 「あいまい（曖昧）」, “vague”.
The two factors are usually similar in nature and able to strengthen each other.
Written style, common in news reports, commentary, and explanatory writing.

daily.title: Sharing a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend how great the trip was.
daily.example: With the great weather on top of everything, it was the best day ever.

daily.title: After a movie
daily.description: Talking about a movie with a friend.
daily.example: The acting and the music together made me cry before I knew it.

work.title: News report
work.description: Analyzing why a product is selling well.
work.example: Together with growing health awareness, sales of this product are rising.

work.title: Report analysis
work.description: Explaining in a report why results declined.
work.example: With soaring raw material prices adding to it, profits fell sharply.

etymology: 「相まつ（相俟つ）」 means “to wait on each other” or “to depend on each other”, and came to mean “to complement each other”. Its te-form 「相まって」 is used as a set connecting expression.

similar.title: 〜に加えて
similar.explanation: 「〜に加えて」 simply adds one more item. 「〜と相まって」 stresses that the two interact and create a stronger effect.

similar.title: 〜こともあって
similar.explanation: 「〜こともあって」 gives one of several reasons in a plain tone. 「〜も相まって」 stresses that this factor stacks with others to make the result more striking.

meaning: “Because it is ... (a special situation)”. Shows that because of a special circumstance, a matching result naturally follows.
connection: Noun / plain form + とあって; Noun / plain form + とあっては

senses.label: Because it is ...
senses.meaning: The first part is a special, noteworthy situation, and the second part is the result that naturally follows. Mostly used to describe a scene objectively and common in news reports.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + とあって (common: 「連休とあって」, 「〜が来るとあって」)
examples: Since it's a long weekend, tourist spots are packed everywhere.
Because a popular singer was coming, a long line formed at the venue from the morning.
It's her first trip abroad, so my daughter is very excited.

senses.label: If it's ..., then (I have to)
senses.meaning: 「〜とあっては」 means “if it's this special situation”. It is usually followed by a reluctant judgment like “I have no choice but to ...” or “I can't not ...”.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + とあっては (often followed by 「〜わけにはいかない」 or 「〜しかない」)
examples: If it's an order from the president, I can't refuse to follow it.
If it's a request from a dear friend, I can't say no.

notes: The second part is usually an objective description. It doesn't take the speaker's own intention, commands, or requests (✕「連休とあって、出かけよう」).
The first part must be a special or unusual situation, not an everyday matter.
「〜とあっては」 is close to 「〜とあれば」, but 「〜とあっては」 more often leads to a negative or reluctant result.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A TV report shows holiday crowds.
daily.example: Since it's the end of the year, the shopping street is bustling with shoppers.

daily.title: Chatting with family
daily.description: Talking about how a child is preparing for exams.
daily.example: It's his first entrance exam, so my son studies late every night.

daily.title: Agreeing to help a friend
daily.description: An old friend asks for help, and you feel you can't refuse.
daily.example: If it's you asking, I can't really say no.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report from a new product launch.
work.example: Because it was a limited-edition release, some people even lined up overnight in front of the store.

work.title: Taking on an urgent task
work.description: Responding when the department head personally assigns a task.
work.example: Since the request comes from you personally, I can't possibly turn it down.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「あって」, the te-form of 「ある」. It originally meant “(the situation) is ..., and so”. 「とある」 presents a particular situation; with 「て」 it gives a reason, and with 「ては」 a condition.

similar.title: 〜だけあって
similar.explanation: 「〜だけあって」 means “as you'd expect from ...”: the result fits the person's status or effort, and it carries praise. 「〜とあって」 just explains the result of a special situation.

similar.title: 〜とあれば
similar.explanation: 「〜とあれば」 usually means “if it's for ..., I'm willing to do it” and leads to a positive intention. 「〜とあっては」 usually leads to a reluctant “I have no choice but to”.

similar.title: 〜こともあって
similar.explanation: 「〜こともあって」 gives one of several reasons. 「〜とあって」 stresses that the situation is special and attention-grabbing.

meaning: “If it's (for) ..., then ...”. Shows a willingness to act for a special reason or in a special situation.
connection: Noun / plain form + とあれば

senses.label: If it's for ...
senses.meaning: The first part is a very important reason or person. The second part shows you are willing to do anything or make any sacrifice for it. Often paired with 「〜のため」 or 「〜の頼み」.
senses.connection: Noun (のため／の頼み) + とあれば (common: 「子供のためとあれば」)
examples: If it's for their children, parents will endure any hardship.
If you're the one asking, I can't really say no.
If it's an order from the president, we have no choice but to follow it.

senses.label: If ... is needed
senses.meaning: Means “if there is such a situation or need”. Mostly used in set phrases like 「必要とあれば」, with a formal tone.
senses.connection: Noun + とあれば (common: 「必要とあれば」, 「ご希望とあれば」)
examples: Please contact us at any time if necessary.
If you wish, we will send you the materials.

notes: The second part is usually the speaker's positive intention, resolve, or ability (「〜もいとわない」, 「何でもする」).
「〜とあらば」 is a more classical version with the same meaning.
Compared with 「〜なら」, 「〜とあれば」 implies that the first part is a special or important case, and the tone is more formal.

daily.title: A parent talks about their child
daily.description: A mother talks about how far she'll go for her child.
daily.example: If it's for my daughter's dream, I plan to support her in anything.

daily.title: Agreeing to help a friend
daily.description: A friend asks for help moving.
daily.example: If my best friend is asking, I'm happy to help.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Offering further help to a client.
work.example: Should you require it, our representative will visit you to explain.

work.title: Accepting extra work
work.description: Willing to make sacrifices for an important project.
work.example: If it's for the company's survival, I'm prepared to work on my days off too.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「あれば」, the conditional of 「ある」. It originally meant “if (the situation) is ...”. The classical form is 「とあらば」.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「〜なら」 is a general condition. 「〜とあれば」 stresses that the first part is a special, important reason, and the second part is usually resolve to make an effort.

similar.title: 〜とあっては
similar.explanation: 「〜とあっては」 usually leads to a reluctant “I have no choice but to”. 「〜とあれば」 usually leads to a positive intention.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 「〜ために」 simply shows purpose. 「〜のためとあれば」 carries the strong resolve “if it's for this, I'll do anything”.

meaning: “Both A and B ...; whether it's A or B ...”. Gives two examples to show that the whole thing has a certain quality.
connection: Noun A + といい、Noun B + といい

senses.label: Both A and B
senses.meaning: Picks two aspects of the same thing as representatives to say “no matter how you look at it, ...”. It is followed by the speaker's evaluation, which can be positive or negative, and often sounds admiring or fed up.
senses.connection: Noun A + といい、Noun B + といい、(evaluation)
examples: Both the taste and the price are perfect at this restaurant.
Both the color and the design make this dress perfect for her.
My dad, my older brother... the men in my family are all stubborn.

notes: A and B must be nouns, and they are different aspects of the same thing or things of the same kind.
The second part is the speaker's subjective evaluation. It doesn't take intentions or requests.
Don't confuse it with 「〜といい」 (“it would be good if ...”), which is a suggestion or wish.

daily.title: Praising a restaurant
daily.description: Thoughts after a meal with a friend.
daily.example: Between the atmosphere and the service, it's a place that makes you want to come back.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Grumbling after bad weather day after day.
daily.example: Yesterday, today... nothing but rain. I'm sick of it.

daily.title: Complimenting a child
daily.description: Seeing that a friend's child is very well-behaved.
daily.example: From the way he speaks to his manners, your son is really mature.

work.title: Evaluating a plan
work.description: Supporting a proposal in a meeting.
work.example: In terms of both cost and schedule, this plan is the most realistic.

work.title: Evaluating an employee
work.description: A manager praises a new hire after a meeting.
work.example: Both his planning skills and his presentation skills are beyond what we expected.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「いい」, the stem form of 「言う」. Literally “speaking of A, speaking of B”. Listing two aspects side by side came to mean “whether A or B, both ...”.

similar.title: 〜といわず〜といわず
similar.explanation: 「〜といわず〜といわず」 means “not just A or B, but everywhere”, stressing that something covers the whole range. 「〜といい〜といい」 stresses that two representative aspects share a quality, followed by an evaluation.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ
similar.explanation: 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 means “whether A or B (the conclusion is the same)” and can take verbs. 「〜といい〜といい」 only takes nouns and is followed by an evaluation.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「〜やら〜やら」 lists a few examples out of many: “what with A and B”. 「〜といい〜といい」 focuses on evaluation.

meaning: “About ...; at most ...”. Says that an amount or degree isn't very high, or gives a rough assessment of the current state.
connection: Noun / quantity / plain form + といったところだ

senses.label: At most ...
senses.meaning: Shows that an amount or degree is roughly in a certain range, and that it isn't much or very high. Often used with 「せいぜい」, 「多くても」, or 「〜程度」.
senses.connection: Quantity + といったところだ (common: 「せいぜい〜といったところだ」)
examples: There will be 30 participants at most.
I get five hours of sleep at most.

senses.label: Roughly ...; I'd say ...
senses.meaning: Gives a rough, somewhat reserved assessment of the current state: “you could say it's like ...”. In speech, 「〜ってところだ」 and 「〜といったところかな」 are common.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + といったところだ／ってところだ
examples: This year's results were so-so, I'd say.
I'd say I've recovered about 80 percent.
I'd say I'm feeling great.

notes: Since it means “not much”, it doesn't work for stressing a large amount (✕「参加者は1万人といったところだ」 sounds odd if you mean “a lot”).
Don't confuse it with 「〜と言ったところ、〜」 (“when I said ..., then ...”), which describes what happened after saying something.
「〜といったところで」 (“even if you say ...”) is a different grammar point.

daily.title: Talking about income
daily.description: A friend asks how much your part-time job pays.
daily.example: My part-time job pays about 50,000 yen a month.

daily.title: Giving an update
daily.description: A friend asks how you're settling into a new job.
daily.example: I'm getting used to it, but I'd say I'm still only halfway there.

work.title: Reporting progress
work.description: Reporting project progress to your manager.
work.example: We're about 60 percent of the way through overall.

work.title: Forecasting sales
work.description: Estimating a new product's sales in a meeting.
work.example: First-month sales will probably be a thousand units at most.

etymology: From 「と言った」 (“said like that”) plus the formal noun 「ところ」 (“extent, stage”) and the copula 「だ」. Literally “it's at the stage where you could say ...”, which became “roughly at the level of ...”.

similar.title: 〜くらいのものだ
similar.explanation: 「〜くらいのものだ」 means “only ... does that”, stressing that something is the only one. 「〜といったところだ」 says the degree is roughly this much.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: 「〜にすぎない」 states firmly “it's nothing more than ...” and sounds dismissive. 「〜といったところだ」 is a softer estimate.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: 「〜くらい」 simply shows an approximate amount. 「〜といったところだ」 adds the judgment that it “isn't much”.

meaning: “Even ...; although ...”. Accepts a status or fact in the first part, but the second part goes against what you'd normally expect.
connection: Noun / plain form + といえども

senses.label: Even ...
senses.meaning: Names a special status or position to say “even such a person is no exception”. The second part is usually an obligation, claim, or evaluation. Written style with a formal tone.
senses.connection: Noun + といえども (common: 「いかに〜といえども」, 「たとえ〜といえども」)
examples: Even a child is held responsible for breaking the law.
Even a master sometimes fails.

senses.label: Although ...
senses.meaning: Accepts the first part as fact, but the second part doesn't match it. Similar to 「〜とはいえ」 but stiffer.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + といえども
examples: Although it's spring according to the calendar, the cold days continue.
Although the economy has recovered, life is still hard.

senses.label: Not even one ...
senses.meaning: Follows the smallest amount, like 「一円」 or 「一日」, and is followed by a negative: “not even a little”.
senses.connection: 一 + counter + といえども + negative
examples: Not even a single yen of tax money may be wasted.
I can't skip practice even for a single day.

notes: Written style, mostly seen in law, news, and speeches. It sounds stiff in everyday conversation.
The second part is usually the speaker's judgment, an obligation, or a claim.
Often paired with 「いかに」, 「たとえ」, or 「いくら」 to strengthen the concession.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: An old man lectures a young man in a novel.
daily.example: Even between close friends, there are things you can say and things you can't.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report about the seasonal weather.
daily.example: Although it was October, the daytime heat felt like midsummer.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: HR explains the rules to employees.
work.example: Even executives must follow company regulations.

work.title: Budget meeting
work.description: The finance manager stresses cost-cutting.
work.example: We must not waste even one yen of expenses.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」, 「言え」 (the realis form of 「言う」), and the classical conjunction 「ども」 (“although”). Literally “although it is said to be ...”. It keeps a concessive use from classical Japanese.

similar.title: 〜とはいえ
similar.explanation: 「〜とはいえ」 is mostly a factual concession, “although ...”, and works in both writing and speech. 「〜といえども」 is stiffer and also often means “even ...”.

similar.title: 〜とて
similar.explanation: 「〜とて」 also means “even ...”, usually after a person (「私とて」), and is emotional. 「〜といえども」 is more objective and formal.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 「〜ても」 is a general concessive condition. 「〜といえども」 is written style, and its first part is usually a special status or fact.

meaning: “Incredibly ...; beyond words”. Shows that a degree is extremely high, too high to put into words.
connection: Noun / i-adjective + といったらない; i-adjective + ったらない

senses.label: Beyond words
senses.meaning: Shows that a feeling or state is so intense it can't be described. It works for both positive and negative things. It often follows a noun ending in 「〜さ」.
senses.connection: Noun (adjective + さ) / i-adjective + といったらない（なかった）
examples: The view from the summit was more beautiful than words can say.
The loneliness of staying home alone is just indescribable.
You should have seen how happy he was.

senses.label: Casual: so ... it's unbearable
senses.meaning: In speech it becomes 「〜ったらない」 or 「〜ったらありゃしない」. Mostly used for complaints: “so ... it's unbearable”.
senses.connection: i-adjective + ったらない／ったらありゃしない
examples: The construction next door is so noisy I can't stand it.
I fell over in front of everyone. It was so embarrassing.

notes: 「〜といったらない」 can be positive or negative, but 「〜ったらありゃしない」 is basically only negative.
Don't confuse it with 「〜といったら」 (“speaking of ...”), which raises a topic. In this pattern, 「ない」 or another negative always follows.
For a past feeling, use 「〜といったらなかった」.

daily.title: Sharing a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about seeing the northern lights.
daily.example: When I saw the aurora for the first time, I was moved beyond words.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Waiting for a bus outside on a hot summer day.
daily.example: This heat is unbelievable. I feel like I'm melting.

daily.title: Venting about someone
daily.description: Complaining about someone with friends.
daily.example: That person talks forever. It's unbearable.

work.title: Looking back on a project
work.description: Looking back on the hard times at a celebration party.
work.example: We were insanely busy right before the deadline, weren't we?

work.title: Book review
work.description: A review praising a work.
work.example: The intricate structure of this work is simply magnificent.

etymology: From 「と言ったら」 (“if you tried to say ...”) plus 「ない」. Literally “if you tried to put it into words, there are none”, which means “indescribable”, and so shows an extreme degree.

similar.title: 〜極まる／〜極まりない
similar.explanation: 「〜極まりない」 follows na-adjectives, is written style, and is mostly negative. 「〜といったらない」 works in both speech and writing and can be positive or negative.

similar.title: 〜ことこの上ない
similar.explanation: 「〜ことこの上ない」 is written style: “nothing could be more ...”. 「〜といったらない」 sounds more like an exclamation.

similar.title: 〜といったら (raising a topic)
similar.explanation: On its own, 「〜といったら」 means “speaking of ...”. Only when 「ない」 follows does it become this pattern, showing an extreme degree.

meaning: “As for ... (honestly!)”. Brings up a topic, usually followed by dissatisfaction, criticism, or exasperation.

senses.label: As for ... (complaint)
senses.meaning: Brings up a person or thing close to you as a topic, then follows with the speaker's dissatisfaction or complaint. Casual and mostly spoken.
senses.connection: Noun + ときたら (common: 「うちの〜ときたら」, 「最近の〜ときたら」)
examples: My husband, honestly. On his days off he just sleeps all day.
Young people these days can't even use keigo properly.
This room is cramped, and on top of that it gets hardly any sunlight.

senses.label: When it comes to ..., nothing beats ...
senses.meaning: Brings up a topic, then says what goes best with it: “speaking of this, of course you think of ...”. The tone is light.
senses.connection: Noun + ときたら、(やっぱり) 〜だ
examples: When it comes to summer nights, nothing beats an ice-cold beer.
When it comes to sushi, this place is the best.

notes: Mainly used for people and things close to the speaker. The second part is usually a complaint or criticism, and it is almost never used to praise others.
Spoken expression. Not used in formal documents.
「〜ときた日には」 is also used and sounds even more dissatisfied.

daily.title: Complaining about a child
daily.description: A mother complains to a friend about her son.
daily.example: My son, honestly. He does nothing but play games and never studies.

daily.title: Venting about the train
daily.description: The train is late again during the morning rush.
daily.example: This line is late practically every morning.

daily.title: Drinks with friends
daily.description: Talking about a favorite bar snack.
daily.example: When it comes to yakitori, it's got to be beer.

work.title: Complaining among coworkers
work.description: Complaining about the boss with coworkers over lunch.
work.example: Our department head is always late to meetings.

work.title: Complaining about equipment
work.description: The office copier has broken down again.
work.example: This copier always breaks down right when you need it most.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「来たら」, the conditional of 「来る」. Literally “if (the topic) comes to ...”. It is usually written in kana and brings up a topic, mostly followed by a complaint.

similar.title: 〜といったら (raising a topic)
similar.explanation: 「〜といったら」 raises a topic and can be followed by a neutral or positive evaluation. 「〜ときたら」 is usually followed by dissatisfaction or criticism.

similar.title: 〜くせに
similar.explanation: 「〜くせに」 means “even though ...” and criticizes a contradiction. 「〜ときたら」 first names the topic, then complains about it.

similar.title: 〜に至っては
similar.explanation: 「〜に至っては」 picks out the most extreme example in a list and is written style. 「〜ときたら」 is spoken and raises a single topic.

meaning: “Even ...; even if ...”. Shows that even from a certain position, or even assuming a certain situation, the result won't change.
connection: Noun + にしたところで; plain form + としたところで

senses.label: Even (for) ...
senses.meaning: Names a person or position to say “even from ...'s point of view, it's the same”. The second part is usually a negative judgment.
senses.connection: Noun (person, organization) + にしたところで (common: 「私にしたところで」, 「社長にしたところで」)
examples: Even the president probably can't solve this problem easily.
Speaking for myself, it's not that I don't understand how he feels.

senses.label: Even if ...
senses.meaning: Assumes a situation and says “even then, things won't get better”. The second part is usually a negative guess. Often paired with 「仮に」 or 「たとえ」.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form (usually the ta-form) + としたところで
examples: Even if we hurry now, we probably won't make the last train.
Even if he did apologize, I don't think he'd be forgiven.

notes: The second part is usually a negative judgment, meaning “the result won't change”.
In speech, 「〜にしたって」 and 「〜としたって」 are also common.
Don't confuse it with 「〜しようとしたところで」 (“just as I was about to ...”), where 「ところで」 is about time.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend regrets not leaving earlier.
daily.example: Even if we'd left earlier, it would have been the same in this traffic.

daily.title: Family discussion
daily.description: Discussing whether to ask Dad for advice.
daily.example: Even Dad, I don't think he'd have any good ideas.

work.title: Project discussion
work.description: Discussing whether pushing back the deadline would help.
work.example: Even if we extend the deadline by a week, the quality won't necessarily improve.

work.title: Understanding the boss's position
work.description: A coworker privately explains the manager's difficult position.
work.example: Even the department head can't go against orders from above, you know.

etymology: From the ta-form of 「とする／にする」 (“to take as, to regard as”) plus the conjunction 「ところで」 (“even if”). Literally “even if you take ... as given”, which expresses a concession.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: 「〜たところで」 follows the verb ta-form and means “even if you do it, it's no use”. 「〜にしたところで」 usually follows a noun and means “even from ...'s standpoint”.

similar.title: 〜にしても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「〜にしても」 is used more widely, while 「〜にしたところで」 more strongly suggests “the result won't change”.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: 「〜としても」 is a general concessive condition. 「〜としたところで」 implies the negative judgment “even then, it's no use”.

title: 〜とは (surprise)
meaning: “To think that ...!”. Shows surprise or strong feelings about an unexpected fact. The rest of the sentence is often left out.

senses.label: To think that ...!
senses.meaning: Expresses surprise, emotion, or indignation at something unexpected. The second half is often left out, or followed by a reaction like 「驚いた」 or 「残念だ」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは（。）／とは、+ reaction
examples: I never imagined he was the culprit.
Fancy meeting you in a place like this. What a surprise!
To think we lost after practicing that much. It's so frustrating.

senses.label: I never thought ...
senses.meaning: In forms like 「〜とは思わなかった」 or 「〜とは夢にも思わなかった」, it shows something was completely unexpected. It is stronger than 「〜と思わなかった」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは + 思わなかった／夢にも思わなかった
examples: I never thought those two would get married.
I never dreamed I'd win the lottery.

notes: Often paired with 「まさか」, 「あんなに」, or 「こんなに」 to stress how unexpected something is.
In casual speech, 「〜なんて」 is common. 「〜とは」 is a bit more formal.
It looks the same as 「〜とは」 for definitions (“... means ...”). Check whether what follows is an explanation or an exclamation.

daily.title: Hearing unexpected news
daily.description: Learning that a friend suddenly quit his job.
daily.example: To think that someone as serious as him would quit his job.

daily.title: Running into an old classmate
daily.description: Bumping into an elementary school classmate abroad.
daily.example: I never thought I'd run into you here!

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: The hero of a novel learns the truth.
daily.example: I never dreamed I'd be betrayed by a friend I trusted.

work.title: Surprised by the outcome
work.description: When a proposal is unexpectedly accepted.
work.example: I was surprised that a new hire's proposal actually got chosen.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator talks about an unexpected event.
work.example: No one expected that such a long-established company would go bankrupt so easily.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」 plus the topic particle 「は」, originally marking “the fact that ...”. Words like 「驚いた」 or 「思わなかった」 that followed were often dropped, so 「〜とは」 on its own took on a tone of surprise.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: 「〜なんて」 is casual and can also sound dismissive. 「〜とは」 is more formal and mainly expresses surprise or strong feelings.

similar.title: 〜とは (definition)
similar.explanation: For a definition, 「〜とは」 is followed by an explanation (「〜とは〜のことだ」). For surprise, it is followed by a reaction or nothing at all.

meaning: “Although ...; even so”. Accepts the first part as fact while pointing out another side that doesn't match it or needs attention.
connection: Noun / plain form + とはいえ; 「とはいえ」 as a conjunction at the start of a sentence

senses.label: Although ...
senses.meaning: Accepts the first part as true, but the second part differs from what you'd expect. The second part is usually the speaker's opinion or judgment. Used in writing and formal speech.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + とはいえ (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns and na-adjectives)
examples: It may be spring, but mornings and evenings are still cold.
You may be busy with work, but you could at least get in touch.
I understand it in my head, but it's hard to actually do it.

senses.label: Even so
senses.meaning: Placed at the start of a sentence as a conjunction, linking to what came before: “that said, ...”. Often used to add a reservation or a warning.
senses.connection: Previous sentence。+ とはいえ、〜
examples: The plan is going smoothly. That said, we can't let our guard down.
The exam is over. Even so, I can't relax until the results come out.

notes: 「〜とはいえない」 (“can't be called ...”) is a negative expression, not this pattern.
The second part is the speaker's opinion or judgment. Commands and requests are less common.
It can also be written in kanji as 「とは言え」.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with family before heading out in the morning.
daily.example: It may be March, but you still need a coat.

daily.title: Feeling guilty
daily.description: Eating dessert again while on a diet.
daily.example: It may be the weekend, but I think I ate a bit too much.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report that the economy is improving.
daily.example: The economy is on a recovery trend. Even so, the burden on households remains heavy.

work.title: Project meeting
work.description: Reminding the team not to get careless.
work.example: Sales hit the target. That said, there are still many issues.

work.title: Coaching a new hire
work.description: Explaining responsibility to a new hire who made a mistake.
work.example: You may be new, but to the customer you're a professional.

etymology: Made from the quoting particle 「と」, the topic particle 「は」, and 「言え」, the realis form of 「言う」. In classical Japanese the realis form alone could express “although”, so it literally means “although it is said that ...”.

similar.title: 〜といえども
similar.explanation: 「〜といえども」 is stiffer and can also mean “even ...”. 「〜とはいえ」 is mainly a concession that accepts a fact, and it is used more widely.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「〜ものの」 usually follows verbs or adjectives, and the second part is often “but couldn't do it”. With 「〜とはいえ」, the second part is usually the speaker's opinion or judgment.

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: 「〜といっても」 is often used to correct high expectations (「旅行といっても近場だ」). 「〜とはいえ」 focuses on “it's true, but ...”.

similar.title: 〜ながら（も）
similar.explanation: 「〜ながらも」 usually follows verbs or adjectives, with the same subject in both parts. 「〜とはいえ」 connects more freely and can also be a conjunction.
